name: Red Hat OpenShift (Harbor backend)

modes.label: OpenShift Dedicated worker subscription component
modes.commit_note: $0.171 per 4 vCPU-hour equivalent; customers billed annually. 1-year $0.114/4-vCPU-h; 3-year $0.076/4-vCPU-h. Infrastructure and minimum worker configuration extra.

plans.name: Public rate not established
plans.note: Unknown limits are not promises of unlimited capacity.

plans.name: Developer Sandbox
plans.note: Pods deleted after 12 consecutive hours; Linux VMs shut down after one hour; shared multitenant evaluation only. Resource quota per user (Red Hat blog, 2024-05): one project, 3 cores, 14 GB RAM, 40 GB storage.

caveats: Harbor adapter runs workload on customer OpenShift cluster. Licence/controlplane and worker infrastructure are not free or included in a universal sandbox hourlyprice.
Not fully priceable in ENGINE_CARD: unknown USD resource rates or machine shape. Null is not zero; do not rank as a free provider.

Features set to null were not verified. No sandbox was purchased or tested; feature/performance statements are documentation claims. Null maximums are unknown unless a cited note explicitly states unlimited.
A complete monthly bill requires known snapshot/egress/plan limits; do not silently treat missing ancillary charges as free.

audit_2026_09_29.source: checked against the provider's live pricing and docs pages

snapshot_auto.quote: The lifetime of this ephemeral storage does not extend beyond the life of the individual pod, and this ephemeral storage cannot be shared across pods.
snapshot_auto.note: Card models Harbor running plain Pods (restartPolicy Never) on a customer OCP cluster. No save-on-stop: the container filesystem is discarded with the pod; only PVC data persists. No idle/stop checkpointing in OCP.

snapshot_on_demand.quote: A snapshot represents the state of the storage volume in a cluster at a particular point in time. Volume snapshots can be used to provision a new volume.
snapshot_on_demand.note: CSI VolumeSnapshot of PVCs only (requires a snapshot-capable CSI driver; 'Cloning and snapshotting is disabled for disks with ReadWriteMany access mode enabled' for some drivers). Container root fs and memory not captured; restore = new PVC for a new pod. (OpenShift Virtualization VMs have their own VM snapshots; not used by the Harbor backend.)

harness_api.quote: Red Hat OpenShift icon Cloud, Containers, Kubernetes Red Hat OpenShift Build, modernize, and deploy apps at scale.
harness_api.note: OpenShift is a generic Kubernetes/container application platform, not an AI-agent sandbox product; Red Hat ships no first-party API to prompt, stream events to, or send follow-ups to a coding-agent harness running inside a pod. The only harness-driving mechanism modeled in the card is Harbor's own third-party adapter (oc exec), which is not first-party. No official Red Hat page documents any such API, consistent with the existing 'no evidence' claim.

egress_allowlist.quote: As a cluster administrator, you can use an egress firewall to limit the external hosts that some or all pods can access from within the cluster. [...] The egress firewall matches network traffic that meets any of the following criteria: An IP address range in CIDR format A DNS name that resolves to an IP address A port number
egress_allowlist.note: EgressFirewall CR (OVN-Kubernetes) is per project/namespace (max one CR, 8,000 rules), cluster-admin only, supports dnsName incl. wildcards; NetworkPolicy egress rules give per-pod IP/port control. Enforced by OVN outside the pod. Caveat: 'Egress firewall rules do not apply to traffic that goes through routers.' Harbor's adapter declares network_allowlist=False (does not configure it).

ingress_rules.quote: haproxy.router.openshift.io/ip_allowlist Sets an allowlist for the route. The allowlist is a space-separated list of IP addresses and CIDR ranges for the approved source addresses. Requests from IP addresses that are not in the allowlist are dropped.
ingress_rules.note: Ports are only exposed externally if you create a Service/Route; NetworkPolicy ingress rules isolate pods ('you can create NetworkPolicy objects in that project to indicate the allowed incoming connections'); Route IP allowlists; LB allowedSourceRanges.

guest_firewall.quote: You can drop all capabilites from containers by setting the requiredDropCapabilities parameter to ALL. This is what the restricted-v2 SCC does.
guest_firewall.note: Pods under restricted-v2 (and Harbor's custom harbor-task-scc: requiredDropCapabilities ALL, adds only CHOWN/DAC_OVERRIDE/FOWNER/FSETID/KILL/NET_BIND_SERVICE/SETGID/SETUID/SYS_CHROOT) lack NET_ADMIN, so iptables/nftables inside fail. A cluster admin could grant NET_ADMIN via a custom SCC, or use OpenShift Virtualization / Sandboxed Containers (Kata VMs).

secret_proxy.quote: The Secret object type provides a mechanism to hold sensitive information such as passwords, OpenShift Container Platform client configuration files, private source repository credentials, and so on. Secrets decouple sensitive content from the pods.
secret_proxy.note: Secrets are mounted as files or env vars into the pod (also Secrets Store CSI driver from external vaults); no credential-injecting egress proxy.

volume_attach.quote: Pods use claims as volumes. The cluster inspects the claim to find the bound volume and mounts that volume for a pod.
volume_attach.note: PersistentVolumeClaims mounted into pods (block/file, depends on cluster storage). Harbor's SCC allows persistentVolumeClaim volumes, but its pod spec mounts none by default.

volume_shared.quote: The volume can be mounted as read/write by many nodes.
volume_shared.note: ReadWriteMany (RWX) PVCs, read-write, when the storage backend supports it (e.g. NFS, CephFS/ODF); ReadOnlyMany also available.

isolation.quote: The container runtime is responsible for running containers. OpenShift Container Platform deploys the CRI-O container runtime on each of the Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS (RHCOS) nodes in your cluster.
isolation.note: Card models Harbor running plain Pods on OCP: CRI-O containers sharing the node kernel (SCC-restricted). OpenShift Virtualization/OpenShift sandboxed containers (Kata) exist as optional add-ons but are not what the Harbor 'cluster' mode uses.

image_oci.quote: A pod consists of one or more containers to run in a worker node.
image_oci.note: Pods run arbitrary OCI/Docker images pulled from any registry (ImageStreams, pull secrets, etc.); matches card's existing custom_image:true.

docker_inside.quote: OpenShift Container Platform deploys the CRI-O container runtime on each of the Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS (RHCOS) nodes in your cluster.
docker_inside.note: Node runtime is CRI-O, not Docker; default restricted-v2 SCC (and Harbor's harbor-task-scc) drops capabilities and forbids privileged containers, so running a Docker daemon or docker-in-docker inside a pod is not available without a cluster-admin-granted privileged SCC.

nested_virt.quote: KubeVirt device plugins: vfio and kvm
nested_virt.note: /dev/kvm is exposed to KubeVirt's own VM launcher pods via a device plugin, not to ordinary customer pods; the SCC used by Harbor pods has no NET_ADMIN/device access, so /dev/kvm is not available inside a generic pod.

desktop.quote: Build modern, cloud-native applications on a single, centralized platform with Kubernetes at its core.
desktop.note: not offered: outside the product's scope (OpenShift is a Kubernetes application/container platform; it has no built-in VNC/RDP desktop streaming for workload pods).

browser.quote: Build modern, cloud-native applications on a single, centralized platform with Kubernetes at its core.
browser.note: not offered: outside the product's scope; no managed/real browser is bundled with the platform.

computer_use.quote: Build modern, cloud-native applications on a single, centralized platform with Kubernetes at its core.
computer_use.note: not offered: outside the product's scope; there is no screenshot/click desktop-driving API.

anti_bot.quote: Build modern, cloud-native applications on a single, centralized platform with Kubernetes at its core.
anti_bot.note: not offered: outside the product's scope (generic Kubernetes application platform, not a browsing/scraping product).

captcha_solving.quote: Build modern, cloud-native applications on a single, centralized platform with Kubernetes at its core.
captcha_solving.note: not offered: outside the product's scope.

egress_ip_type.note: Cluster egress traffic goes out through cloud-provider/datacenter node IPs (AWS/Azure/GCP/on-prem); the EgressIP CR lets you pin a namespace's egress to a specific one of those datacenter IPs, but the address itself is still a regular datacenter IP, not residential/mobile.

ssh.note: Interactive/command access to a running pod is via the `oc exec` / `oc rsh` API (over the Kubernetes API server), not a direct SSH daemon in the container; SSH is only used to reach cluster nodes for infra administration, not the Harbor task pod.

snapshot.quote: A snapshot represents the state of the storage volume in a cluster at a particular point in time. Volume snapshots can be used to provision a new volume.
snapshot.note: CSI VolumeSnapshot only covers PersistentVolumeClaims (disk); the ephemeral container root filesystem and running-process memory are not captured ('The lifetime of this ephemeral storage does not extend beyond the life of the individual pod').

fork.quote: A pod is the smallest logical unit in Kubernetes. A pod consists of one or more containers to run in a worker node.
fork.note: No API clones a running pod/machine into a new one with its state; you can only create a new pod from the same image/spec (a fresh instance, not a fork).

fork_running.quote: A pod is the smallest logical unit in Kubernetes.
fork_running.note: No live-clone-without-stopping capability exists for pods.

memory_snapshot_fork.quote: The lifetime of this ephemeral storage does not extend beyond the life of the individual pod, and this ephemeral storage cannot be shared across pods.
memory_snapshot_fork.note: No mechanism captures in-memory process state for cloning; fork is not offered at all so memory-including fork is not offered.

pause_resume.quote: A pod is the smallest logical unit in Kubernetes. A pod consists of one or more containers to run in a worker node.
pause_resume.note: Kubernetes/OpenShift pods can be scaled to 0 replicas (stop, losing in-memory state) or deleted, but there is no pause primitive that freezes and later resumes a running pod's process state.

wake_on_request.quote: A pod is the smallest logical unit in Kubernetes.
wake_on_request.note: Plain OpenShift pods (as Harbor uses them) do not scale-to-zero-and-wake automatically; that behavior exists only in the optional OpenShift Serverless (Knative) add-on, which is not part of the modeled 'cluster' pod mode.

auto_stop_idle.quote: Pods deleted after 12 consecutive hours; Linux VMs shut down after one hour; shared multitenant evaluation only.
auto_stop_idle.note: The idle/session shutdown behavior documented in the card only applies to the free Developer Sandbox trial, not the general paid product; ordinary OpenShift pods run until you stop/delete them (no idle-based auto-stop by default).

live_resize.quote: This mode instructs the VPA to attempt to perform an in-place pod resize when updating CPU or memory resources, where the VPA first attempts to update the resources in a running pod without recreating the pod.
live_resize.note: Vertical Pod Autoscaler InPlaceOrRecreate mode resizes CPU/memory of a running pod without recreating it (falls back to recreate only if in-place is infeasible).

agent_harnesses.quote: Build modern, cloud-native applications on a single, centralized platform with Kubernetes at its core.
agent_harnesses.note: OpenShift is a generic Kubernetes application platform; it does not ship preinstalled coding-agent (Claude Code/Codex/OpenCode) templates. Harbor itself supplies the agent harness on top of OCP, not Red Hat.

own_agent_api.quote: Build modern, cloud-native applications on a single, centralized platform with Kubernetes at its core.
own_agent_api.note: not offered: outside the product's scope; no first-party browser/computer-use/research task-agent API.

mcp_server.quote: Build modern, cloud-native applications on a single, centralized platform with Kubernetes at its core.
mcp_server.note: No official Red Hat OpenShift MCP server for controlling sandboxes was found on the product's own pages as of this check.

lang_python.quote: A pod consists of one or more containers to run in a worker node.
lang_python.note: Pods run any OCI image, including Red Hat's own Universal Base Image (UBI) Python builder/runtime images and Source-to-Image (S2I) Python builders shipped in the OpenShift image streams/catalog; Python is available out of the box via these images.

lang_node.quote: A pod consists of one or more containers to run in a worker node.
lang_node.note: Node.js is available out of the box via Red Hat's UBI Node.js builder/runtime images and Source-to-Image (S2I) Node.js builders in the OpenShift image catalog.

public_ipv4.quote: haproxy.router.openshift.io/ip_allowlist Sets an allowlist for the route.
public_ipv4.note: Pods themselves get only cluster-internal pod IPs; external reachability is via a shared Router/LoadBalancer Service IP or Route hostname, not a dedicated public IPv4 per machine.

inbound_https.quote: haproxy.router.openshift.io/ip_allowlist Sets an allowlist for the route.
inbound_https.note: OpenShift Routes (HAProxy-based router) expose HTTP/HTTPS (edge/passthrough/re-encrypt TLS) URLs to reach services/pods.

egress_http_rules.quote: The egress firewall matches network traffic that meets any of the following criteria: An IP address range in CIDR format A DNS name that resolves to an IP address A port number
egress_http_rules.note: EgressFirewall rules match on IP/CIDR, DNS name, and port number only — there is no HTTP method/path-level egress rule engine.

static_egress_ip.note: The OVN-Kubernetes EgressIP custom resource pins a namespace/pod selector's outbound traffic to a fixed IP address.

gpu.quote: NVIDIA GPU architecture AMD GPU Operator
gpu.note: GPU worker nodes are supported via the NVIDIA GPU Operator and AMD GPU Operator; not the free/default configuration but offered on the platform.

macos.quote: bootupd firmware and boot loader updater: ... modern architectures, such as x86_64, ppc64le, and aarch64.
macos.note: not offered: outside the product's scope; supported node architectures are x86_64, ppc64le, s390x and aarch64 Linux (and Windows worker nodes) — no macOS nodes/machines.

arm64.quote: Installing a cluster with the support for configuring multi-architecture compute machines
arm64.note: OpenShift supports multi-architecture compute (including aarch64/ARM64) clusters and mixed-architecture compute machines.

open_source.quote: OKD is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0.
open_source.note: OpenShift's upstream community distribution, OKD, is Apache-2.0 licensed and open source; Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform is the supported/enterprise distribution built on the same open Kubernetes + OKD components.

soc2.note: Attested for the managed Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS (ROSA) offering; applies to Red Hat's managed OpenShift cloud services.

hipaa.quote: HIPAA Qualified[1] ... Yes ... For more information about Red Hat’s HIPAA Qualified ROSA offerings, see the HIPAA Overview.
hipaa.note: HIPAA-qualified managed OpenShift (ROSA) offering is available; BAA-eligible.

sso.quote: The OpenID Connect is a protocol to authenticate the users to use single sign-on (SSO) to access sites that use OpenID Providers.
sso.note: Built-in OIDC identity provider gives SAML/OIDC-class SSO for cluster (console/oc) access; SAML itself is only available via a community-supported (not Red Hat supported) request-header integration.

eu_data_residency.note: Both self-managed OpenShift Container Platform (deployable on any infrastructure, including EU datacenters) and managed offerings like ROSA support EU regions (e.g. Frankfurt, eu-west-1), keeping clusters/data in the EU.

max_session_h.quote: A pod is the smallest logical unit in Kubernetes. A pod consists of one or more containers to run in a worker node.
max_session_h.note: In the general (paid/self-managed) product, pods and clusters run indefinitely until you stop/delete them — no platform-enforced max session length. The card's Developer Sandbox free-trial plan is a separate, explicitly time-boxed exception (pods deleted after 12 consecutive hours) and is captured there, not as the general product limit.
